questions.stem: Which multiplication has the same answer as 5 + 5?
questions.stemText: Which multiplication has the same answer as 5 + 5 ?
questions.explain: Count the 5s: there are 2 of them, so this is 2 groups of 5, which is 2 × 5 = 10. Counting one group too many gives 3 × 5, which is 5 too much, and multiplying the wrong pair gives 5 × 5 or 3 × 2. Multiplication is a short way of writing the same number added over and over - that is the whole idea, and it is why the times tables are worth knowing by heart.

questions.stem: Farhan works out 5824 + 3614 in columns. One column makes 14, so he writes 4 in that column and a small 1 above the column on its left. How much is the 4 he writes there worth?
questions.stemText: Farhan works out 5824 + 3614 in columns. One column makes 14, so he writes 4 in that column and a small 1 above the column on its left. How much is the 4 he writes there worth?
questions.explain: The column that makes 14 is the hundreds column: 8 + 6 = 14, and no other column reaches ten. 14 hundreds is 1 thousand and 4 hundreds, so the 4 stays in the hundreds column - worth 400 - and the small 1 goes above the thousands column - worth 1000. The 4 is worth 400. A mark is worth the column it is written in, not the digit it looks like: that is what regrouping means, ten of something small becoming one of the next size up. Every wrong answer here is one of the two slips - the right digit read in the wrong column, or the wrong digit read in the right one.

questions.stem: Siti works out 62 + 64 in her head. She makes 70 first. 62 + 64 = 70 + ?
questions.stemText: Siti works out 62 + 64 in her head. She makes 70 first. 62 + 64 = 70 + ?
questions.explain: To get from 62 up to 70 you need 8, so 8 is moved across from the 64. That leaves 64 − 8 = 56, and 70 + 56 = 126. Whatever you give to one number you must take off the other, or the total changes. You could have rounded the 64 up to 70 instead and taken that amount off the 62: it is the same total either way, so it lands on the same answer.

Aisyah makes a pattern of figures with toothpicks.
Figure 1: 3 toothpicks
Figure 2: 12 toothpicks
Figure 3: 21 toothpicks
Figure 4: 30 toothpicks
The pattern goes on in the same way. She has 98 toothpicks and makes just one figure from the pattern. What is the biggest figure number she can make?
questions.stemText: Aisyah makes a pattern of figures with toothpicks. Figure 1: 3 toothpicks Figure 2: 12 toothpicks Figure 3: 21 toothpicks Figure 4: 30 toothpicks The pattern goes on in the same way. She has 98 toothpicks and makes just one figure from the pattern. What is the biggest figure number she can make?
questions.explain: Find the jump first: 3 → 12 → 21 → 30, so each figure uses 9 more toothpicks than the one before. Figure 1 uses 3 toothpicks, so take those away first: 98 − 3 = 95 toothpicks are left for the jumps. 95 ÷ 9 = 10 remainder 5, so there are enough for 10 jumps after Figure 1: that is Figure 11, which uses 93 toothpicks. Figure 12 would need 102, more than she has. The 5 toothpicks left over are not enough for another jump.

questions.stem: Hui Min lays 4 identical rectangular tiles side by side in one row. Together they make a rectangle 36 cm long and 7 cm wide. What is the area of one tile?
questions.stemText: Hui Min lays 4 identical rectangular tiles side by side in one row. Together they make a rectangle 36 cm long and 7 cm wide. What is the area of one tile?
questions.explain: The 4 tiles share the 36 cm length equally, so each tile measures 36 ÷ 4 = 9 cm along the row. Its other side is as wide as the whole row: 7 cm. Area of one tile = 9 × 7 = 63 cm². (The whole rectangle is 36 × 7 = 252 cm², and 252 ÷ 4 = 63 cm² too.)

questions.explain: Walk the eight sides: 4 + 3 + 6 + 3 + 4 + 10 + 14 + 10 = 54 cm. Careful: this notch is in the middle of a side, not at a corner. The 6 cm taken out of the top edge is replaced by the 6 cm along the bottom of the notch, so that part of the walk is unchanged. But the two sides of the notch, 3 cm down and 3 cm back up, are brand new. Perimeter = 2 × (14 + 10) + 2 × 3 = 54 cm. A corner cut leaves the perimeter alone; a middle notch makes it longer.

questions.stem: PQRS is a trapezium in which the side PQ is parallel to the side SR. The side PS and the side QR each join the two parallel sides. ∠P = 63° and ∠Q = 133°. How many degrees larger is ∠S than ∠R?
questions.stemText: PQRS is a trapezium in which the side PQ is parallel to the side SR. The side PS and the side QR each join the two parallel sides. ∠P = 63° and ∠Q = 133°. How many degrees larger is ∠S than ∠R?
questions.explain: ∠P and ∠S are at the ends of PS, which crosses the parallel pair, so ∠S = 180° − 63° = 117°. The same for QR: ∠R = 180° − 133° = 47°. The difference is 117° − 47° = 70°.
